articles.title: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine: The birth of optogenetics, a maturing field
articles.description: What if scientists could temporarily switch off a specific part of the brain, observe how behavior changes, then restore its activity within seconds? For decades, understanding which brain circuits govern learning and memory was constrained by the tools available to neuroscientists. Researchers could administer drugs to suppress neural activity or create lesions to disable certain brain regions. However, these methods still made it difficult to determine precisely when particular neurons were necessary for a behavior. That limitation helped motivate the development of optogenetics, which encompasses techniques that use light-sensitive proteins to activate or inhibit targeted neurons with remarkable precision. The work happened in two stages: Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a type of protein found in the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, and Karl Deisseroth turned the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. Deisseroth demonstrated the technique in rat neurons in 2005; the method was born and adopted the name "optogenetics" in 2006. On Oct. 5, the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Hegemann, Nagel and Deisseroth. The press release described the award as "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." As a point of reference to better understand the significance of the prize and the works' implications for neuroscience, Kishore Kuchibhotla shared his insights. He serves as an associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences; his laboratory uses optogenetics to investigate learning and behavior. In an interview with The News-Letter, Kuchibhotla began by explaining how the optogenetic technique differs from earlier approaches to studying the brain. In one experiment, his laboratory trained mice to respond to certain sounds for a water reward while withholding responses to others. By temporarily silencing the auditory cortex, researchers found that the region was essential during learning but no longer necessary for performing the task once the animals became proficient. This distinction between learning and performance illustrates what optogenetics makes possible. Rather than simply observing neural activity alongside behavior, researchers can manipulate a circuit at a particular moment and test the circuit's contributions. Despite research into this method being limited to only a couple of decades, optogenetics is now used in labs worldwide to probe how the brain works. The technique has also extended far beyond auditory neuroscience, with applications in vision, memory and disease research. When asked about his initial reaction to the Nobel announcement, Kuchibhotla described the discovery awarded as one whose recognition was both exciting and long anticipated. "Over the last 20 years, the techniques have matured so much and the impact they've had on basic neuroscience is so huge that it's by no means a surprise, right?" he said. The three researchers are well-recognized for their work in the field; however, Kuchibhotla also emphasizes that the field's development involved far more than the collaboration of just the three. Ed Boyden, Gero Miesenböck and Ernst Bamberg have also contributed to the earlier discoveries involving microbial rhodopsins. Together, their work illustrates how fundamental research across science can eventually produce tools with applications far beyond their original purpose. For Kuchibhotla, the prize also recognizes the importance of making scientific discoveries accessible. Deisseroth's laboratory helped transform optogenetics from a specialized experimental technique into one that researchers around the world could adopt and expand. Similarly to Kuchibhotla's lab, the influence and adoption of optogenetics also manifests clearly in other labs at Hopkins, such as those led by Patricia Janak and Dr. Solange Brown. Undergraduate students, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers all receive necessary and fundamental training in using optogenetics to investigate neural circuits and their relationships to behavior or participate in experiments that activate or inhibit specific brain regions. However, the accessibility of this technology also creates a responsibility to use it carefully. A common concern is that researchers must avoid manipulating neural activity simply because the technology allows them to do so, but rather design experiments around a specific hypothesis. This distinction matters since greater experimental control does not automatically produce a better understanding of the brain; the value of the technique depends on the questions researchers choose to ask. In terms of the technique's potential commercial applications, there are still challenges of translating optogenetics from controlled laboratory experiments into treatments for human patients. One fundamental obstacle is delivering light to targeted neurons deep within the human brain. Although researchers can manipulate neural circuits in animal experiments, translating those methods into safe, practical treatments requires additional advances. One promising application, however, has already emerged in vision restoration. A 2021 study published in Nature Medicine shows how researchers treated a patient with retinitis pigmentosa, a neurodegenerative eye disease, by introducing a light-sensitive protein into retinal cells and using specialized goggles to deliver visual information through pulses of light. With the goggles, the patient regained a limited ability to perceive, locate and count objects. Though the findings mainly represented an early clinical proof of concept, Kuchibhotla argued that the technique's medical significance may extend beyond treatments directly involving light. Optogenetics may therefore help scientists identify which cells and pathways should be targeted by future therapies, even when those treatments ultimately rely on drugs or other interventions. "[Optogenetics] gives you more precision. It gives you more [cell-type and] temporal specificity so that even if the eventual treatment does not use light or optogenetics, they may have identified the right pathways using optogenetics," Kuchibhotla said. Also noteworthy is the incorporation of more advanced techniques in optogenetic experiments, particularly as researchers develop tools to analyze increasingly complex neural activity. A specific, emerging approach known as holographic optogenetics, combines advanced microscopy with highly targeted stimulation of individual neurons by monitoring activity across thousands of neurons, identifying smaller populations associated with a behavior or disease process and selectively manipulating those cells using patterned light. Kuchibotla even highlighted that artificial intelligence could eventually help interpret these complex recordings and identify relevant neurons. "You can put [holographic optogenetics] potentially into an AI loop with analysis, and you can start [understanding neural circuits] in a more closed loop way," he said. Circling back to Kuchibhotla's respect for this year's prize, he recalled being a graduate student when optogenetics entered its modern era and the excitement surrounding a technique that once seemed closer to science fiction than experimental neuroscience. He also reflected on early-career researchers who helped establish the field, including Boyden and Feng Zhang, whose contributions demonstrated that transformative scientific discoveries do not necessarily require decades of experience. "Don't wait for someone to give you the go-ahead. Figure it out if you have a cool idea," he said. That perspective takes the significance of this year's Nobel Prize beyond its immediate technological contributions. Optogenetics grew from fundamental questions about how microorganisms respond to light into a method that has reshaped the study of the biological brain and neurological disease. Its development depended not only on discoveries across scientific disciplines, but also on researchers willing to pursue ideas whose eventual applications were far from certain.

articles.title: Beabadoobee brings the pylons down at Merriweather Post Pavilion
articles.description: Saturday, Oct. 10 saw the arrival of the immensely popular alternative rock artist beabadoobee accompanied by Wisp, a major figure in the modern shoegaze scene, to Merriweather Post Pavilion. Located about a third of the way between Baltimore and D.C., the October date would be Maryland's turn to house beabadoobee on her tour following the release of her fourth and grungiest studio album, Pylon. Because of the Pavillion's extensive lawn area in addition to reserved seating options, a general admission skylounge, and barrier-access frontstage pit, lawn tickets were able to remain affordable while still providing premium options for fans willing to spend more money. Promptly at 8 p.m., Wisp emerged to widespread applause and the gentle hum of her characteristic dreamy, distorted guitar. Wisp opened her setlist by playing "Enough for you,"a fitting showcase of the specific type of nu-metal infused shoegaze that she is best known for making. With drudging drumlines, sludgy, distorted guitar riffs and her gentle vocals sitting on top of it all, "Enough for you" and the songs that followed were compellingly ethereal, especially for fans of Wisp's overdriven sound. However, her comfort in her sonic identity doesn't always act in her favor, often leaving songs feeling underdeveloped or unremarkable, especially when coupled with the run-of-the-mill writing that populates her songs. Following a brief intermission, the stage lights came back up on a stage newly populated by a giant electrical transmission tower and grassy terrain reminiscent of the Midwestern lowlands as beabadoobee emerged behind her band. The performance kicked off with a series of upbeat and iconic lead guitar parts in "Sun Has Set," "10:36"and "Apple Cider." The energy was so invigorating that even audience members in reserved seating areas couldn't help but get up and continue dancing long past the drop of "10:36." From there, the band continued to electrify the crowd before temporarily taking a break and allowing beabadoobee to bring out her acoustic for a solo performance of "Coffee," an intimate fan-favorite and her first major hit. After commenting on the difficulties of tour and the joy of performing, beabadoobee unveiled her unreleased song, "The Road." With a distinctly Americana-inspired instrumentation and simple yet moving verses about traveling away from home, "The Road" is a pleasant Wilco-esque single distinct from Pylon's grittier feel. The energy continued to pick up as the concert eventually came to a climax with the epic, expansive atmosphere of "In Motion" as beabadoobee repeatedly cried her plea of "gotta get away from here." Throughout the show, there were persistent remarks from nearby audience members that "hope she plays 'Beaches,'" a small child even joining in on the calls. Never one to leave fans disappointed, beabadoobee started her last song with its instantly recognizable four chords to the crowd's absolute elation. After a thrilling guitar solo and a heartfelt crowd-led chorus, beabadoobee thanked the audience and left the stage with the sound of "There She Goes"by the La's marking the end of a brilliant journey. It was on this journey that beabadoobee, her band and the crew transformed the stage from just a series of props to equally part of the performance as the music. From light-up electrical wires to sparking transformers, the stage seemed to come alive in new and creative ways. In fact, beabadoobee centered her interactions with the "decorations" in riveting ways, singing "Powerlines" while standing atop the pylon and delivering the first verse of "Satellite" into the ringing payphone stage left. One might believe that such minute on-stage details would be indistinguishable to audiences in the distant lawn, but fortunately for the masses, the live video of the band displayed on large screens hanging from the pavilion's roof was treated as its own world of artistic expression rather than an afterthought. The stream routinely took the liberty of applying psychedelic effects during slow breakdowns or rapidly switching camera views at the climax of a song, making for a visual treat in and of itself. It is all too easy to think of the concert as a solved event: you get on stage, play music, maybe say the name of the city you're in, and then quietly leave. We in the audience have also grown complacent, coming to expect nothing more - maybe a couple pyrotechnics if we're really lucky. But beabadoobee and the crew at Merriweather Post Pavilion consistently showed that that was not the case. The music can be great, but the visuals can have just as much love and passion poured into their production as anything else. Just know that as beabadoobee is getting bigger and playing increasingly populated venues, she and her creative team are not taking her relevance for granted.

articles.title: This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power
articles.description: This article was originally published by Canary Media. America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation — from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors. Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming. Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocked tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards. For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps — all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations. “This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology. What are variable frequency drives? Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy. VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy. All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email. “We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002. Electric Motors in Nearly Every Factory Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant — whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving — was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues. But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters. Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing up-front costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers. “If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system. The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid — giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers. VFDs Slash Motors’ Electricity Use Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers. “If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee. Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the buildout of gas turbines and power plants. “Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers. Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy. Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

articles.title: Here's to 21
articles.description: Usually, the dream comes and goes but stays long enough. It's me and my mom walking from my grandma's house under a colorful night sky. I can see the stars in the dream. I just need to look up and they are the only thing illuminating the night street. When I wake up, a sudden heavy wave of nostalgia washes over me. This is a memory my mind loves to replay when I am sleeping or daydreaming. Interesting enough, it is the first memory of my childhood, as far back my mind can take me. The beautiful part is, it was my birthday. Of all the memories to engrave into my consciousness, my mind chose that one. Lately, this memory has become a part of me, comforting me as it drifts in and out of thoughts. Time has flown. I am a month away from reaching a milestone someone might say. Turning 21 soon, do I feel any different? Yes, I do. As the date approaches, I decided to walk a memory lane and reminisce about the experiences that have shaped the person I am today. Timeline 1: Bravery of a five-year-old The first day of preschool. I definitely cried. I didn't want my mom to leave me there, and looking back, it was the first time I had ever been separated from her. But I decided to be brave. I dried my tears and continued my day. I met incredible tiny little humans who were my first friends. After that I decided I have a passion for learning and made a promise to myself to continue to learn and educate myself. Proud of my five-year-old self. You did exceptional! Timeline 2: Embracing the unfamiliar Moving to America. Suddenly, the words "new" and "unfamiliar" became the foundation of my vocabulary and my everyday life. This move meant seeing my dad for the first time in person. When I hugged my dad, I felt a tidal wave of emotions hit me. Uniting with someone I had only ever known through phone calls and FaceTime, having him physically in front of me was a new start for my family. When I started school, some kids were incredibly kind, and others were not the best. I cried again, of course. I wanted to leave. But just like in preschool, my determination won, and I stayed. Eventually, I made friends, learned a new language, and got used to my new life. However, puberty happens (which definitely wasn't fun), I moved to New Jersey (which was super fun) and finally, I landed in Maryland. Timeline 3: Heartbreak, euphoria and all the in-between Maryland has been my home for five years now. It's where I met my best friend. We were both new to the state and met in Biology class. Thank you Dr. I, to whom I am still grateful for bringing us together. I grew to truly love this place. Maryland has witnessed my heartbreaks, happiness, grief and now adulthood. It has seen me through many chapters, yet something still feels the same. I could never forget the people and experiences that defined this era. It impacted who I am, but most importantly, it showed me who decided to stay in my life. I have felt raw and vulnerable, grieving people I have lost, meeting new people, starting college. And through it all, I lived to tell the tale. The milestone doesn't stop Time doesn't stop even if there have been days where I wished it would. Some of us lose ourselves as we transition through the stages of life. We become different people. We drift apart, and in a blink of an eye, the people who once knew the sound of our laughter became familiar strangers. It is a mystery of existence how lives can intertwine deeply, only to quietly slip away into the background of our past. To 21: I wish for you to surprise me in this new chapter. And to you dear reader: I wish for you to reach a milestone as well. I want everything life has to give even the hard days because without them, I wouldn't know how to appreciate what I have. Let's all remember, growing is not bound to numbers. Everyday is a fresh milestone in the making. Here's to the next one! Alexandra Garcia Herrera is a sophomore from Laurel, Md. majoring in Chemistry. Her column, "Letter from a Freshman," explores her reflections on what happens outside the syllabus: friendships, identity, grief and growth.

articles.description: Fanned by the fierce Santa Ana winds, the Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state.

articles.title: Political violence: How justifications influence voter approval
articles.description: What happens when political violence is presented as a justified response to threat or injustice coming from an out-group? A study by Ursula Daxecker, director at the Max Planck Institute for Politics and Social Science in Göttingen, and Neeraj Prasad of the University of Amsterdam, published in The Journal of Politics, finds that legitimizing violence can increase public approval of both violence and the parties involved in it. Among BJP supporters, the effect went even further: when violence was portrayed as justified, they were less approving of a peaceful response by their own party.

articles.title: Meet the spacetech CEO who’s betting everything on nuclear micropower
articles.description: Peter Cabauy discusses the engineering, regulation and resilience behind bringing nuclear micropower into the space age.

articles.title: Scientists uncover mystery of how snail shells coil to the right or to the left
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a gene that determines whether Japanese snails develop shells that are left- or right-coiling—with implications for understanding the underlying handedness of our own bodies. The researchers from the University of Nottingham and Tohoku University studied wild Euhadra snails in Japan to understand what makes one snail a mirror image of another.

articles.title: Rabbits were a medieval royal luxury in England—until the Black Death made them commonplace
articles.description: The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species.

articles.title: Astronomer leads global team on NASA mission to create unprecedented view of the early universe
articles.description: A University of Missouri astronomer is leading a team of 130 researchers from 62 institutions—including NASA, the California Institute of Technology, Princeton University and Harvard University—on an ambitious mission to capture an unprecedented view of the early universe.

articles.title: Plants shift gene activity within minutes of entering spaceflight, experiment reveals
articles.description: Plants begin responding to spaceflight almost immediately after leaving Earth, according to a new University of Florida study that captured the earliest stages of biological adaptation during a commercial suborbital mission. Published in the journal npj Microgravity, the study reports the results of an experiment conducted by a UF astronaut during Blue Origin's New Shepard NS-26 flight on Aug. 29, 2024.
